answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Eisenhower spoke the words at the Dartmouth College commencement exercises in Hanover, New Hampshire, on 14 June 1953. The Eisenhower Presidential Library’s own quotations page reproduces the passage and attributes it to those remarks, and Quote Investigator records the earliest press citation as the <cite>New York Times</cite> of 15 June 1953, page 10, column 5. The two sentences here open a four-sentence passage that ends “That should be the only censorship.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Remarks at the Dartmouth College Commencement Exercises
Dwight D. Eisenhower, 34th president of the United States
<cite>New York Times</cite>, 15 June 1953, p. 10, col. 5 — per Quote Investigator

source.excerpt: Don’t join the book burners. Don’t think you are going to conceal faults by concealing evidence that they ever existed. Don’t be afraid to go in your library and read every book, as long as that document does not offend our own ideas of decency. That should be the only censorship.
trail: Eisenhower spoke at the Dartmouth College commencement in Hanover, New Hampshire on 14 June 1953. The Eisenhower Presidential Library’s quotations page ↗ (archived) prints the passage and attributes it to “Remarks at the Dartmouth College Commencement Exercises, Hanover, New Hampshire, 6/14/53”.
Quote Investigator ↗ credits the remark to Eisenhower at Dartmouth and gives the earliest citation as the New York Times of 15 June 1953, page 10, column 5, reproducing these two sentences verbatim.
Wikiquote ↗ carries the same four-sentence passage under the same date and occasion.

The line was printed as ephemera at the time. The Library of Congress holds a 1953 item catalogued as “Don’t join the book burners … Dwight David Eisenhower. Hanover, N. H. Dartmouth College. 1953” ↗ in its Printed Ephemera Collection. Quote Investigator also notes that the line is sometimes reproduced with “book banners” in place of “book burners”; the sources above all read burners.
source.excerptNote: The two sentences this page indexes open the passage. The continuation follows the transcription on the Eisenhower Presidential Library’s quotations page; Quote Investigator reproduces the opening two sentences from the earliest press report.

author.bio: Dwight D. Eisenhower commanded the Allied Expeditionary Force in Europe in the Second World War and served as president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. He gave these remarks at Dartmouth in his first year in office, telling a graduating class to go into the library and read every book — an instruction aimed at a moment when what libraries held had become a political question.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Eisenhower delivered the address in his first year in the White House, at a moment when what American libraries held had become a political question. Quote Investigator ↗, tracing the remark, quotes William Safire’s 1968 account of the period: there was pressure “not only against leftists, liberals, and dissenters in general, but also against the presence of their books in publicly sponsored libraries.”
In the passage itself Eisenhower names no one. The sentence has outlived the argument that produced it, which is why it returns to circulation whenever a library’s shelves become contested ground.
